newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi starts building $323 mln desalination plant.
newsitem.headline: Saudi starts building $323 mln desalination plant.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Abdullah on Tuesday laid the cornerstone of a 1.21 billion riyal ($323 million) desalination plant to meet rising demand for water, the official Saudi Press Agency reported.

Minister of Agriculture and Water Resources Abdullah bin Abdul-Aziz bin Muammar said the project would supply the western provincial cities of Jeddah, Taif and Mecca with 100 million gallons (378.5 million litres) a day of potable water, the agency said.

"The project includes pipelines to transport 60 million gallons of water daily to the governorate of Jeddah, building three main pumping stations in addition to improving present pumping stations used to transport 40 million gallons a day of al-Shuaiba water to Mecca and the governorate of Taif," he said.
"The cost of this project is in excess of 1.211 billion riyals," he added.
Known as Al-Shuaiba Phase Two, the project 110 km (68 miles) south of the Red Sea port city of Jeddah will also generate 500 megawatts of electric power.
Saudi Arabia depends on scarce rainfall, non-renewable underground water and desalination to supply water for its population of 18 million, which is growing at 3.5 to four percent a year.
Desalination capacity in the kingdom, where temperatures soar above 50 Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) in the summer, stands at 520 million gallons daily from 23 plants.
The government plans to lift capacity to 800 million gallons when water projects now being carried out under the 1995-2000 development plan are completed.

The plan said non-renewable ground water supplied about 80 percent of the kingdom's total water needs, with desalination covering only about four percent of the yearly demand estimated at 18.2 billion cubic metres in 1995.
Muammar said his ministry had already launched some 128 water projects -- including dams, wells and pipelines -- at a cost of about 17 billion riyals.

The Saudi government has taken steps, such as a decision a year ago to stop grain exports, to drastically reduce water use. Frequent advertisements on state-run television also call on the public to rein in use of the valuable resource.
